utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I think there are a few procedural issues on our list which we'd like to deal with first. Yes. The first one, that's a question to you, Mr. Stewart. We talked extensively on the Savkic exhibits. 1055 you gave up your -- your objections against admission. It's now both parties want that to have to be admitted. The situation as far as 1056 is concerned is not entirely clear to the Chamber at this moment. It's clear for the other -- the remaining Savkic exhibits, but 1055 and 1056 were, in the past, dealt with very often jointly, so therefore, whether the position taken by the Defence on 1055 is also the position in view of 1056 is not entirely clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is Your Honour asking or expecting an immediate answer, because I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I do not put the question to you, you do not start thinking about answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we get a response this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tieger, there seems to be -- you would like to speak about the Nielsen material. The Chamber inquired into the availability of some of the footnote material from Nielsen, and this may have been understood by you that we wanted to see it all right away, which was not at that moment the request of the Chamber. Is there anything you would like to raise in this respect or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Court's correct, I did interpret that as an implicit request for those materials, if available, although I anticipated the Court might not want all of the available materials, so I can indicate the following to the Court: First, there are materials that fall within the purview of the Court's inquiry. Those have been prepared in, roughly, the following way: With respect to the communications to the Presidency and the government, that is the Prime Minister, those materials have been collected and copied and are available. With respect to the Daily Bulletins, they were more voluminous, as I think the Court was aware, so simply attempted to copy those that seemed most relevant to the Court's request, approximately 20, I think, of the -- of what I understand to be about 80 -- or about a hundred available. So -- and we leave it to the Court, of course, whether it wishes to take those, to request that the additional -- any additional documents that were not copied and made available, but it -- the documents I just indicated are here and are available for the Court's perusal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will further consider the matter, but one solution might be that the parties are invited, for example, to -- to present five or ten of these reports which, in the eyes of the Prosecution, would best support the findings of Mr. Nielsen, whereas the Defence then might try to identify the ones that show that there's no support whatsoever in these reports for what -- for the conclusions of Mr. Nielsen. We're not necessarily -- what we're trying to do very often is to see whether what is presented to us is objectively supported by material that is either specifically relied upon or which, in the view of the Chamber, would be suitable for such support or lack of support. We're always trying to find objective grounds for what has presented to us as opinion or uncorroborated -- corroborated personal observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I completely agree, Your Honour. And as the Court is aware, it was the Prosecution's intention and previous practice to provide the Court with all of the supporting materials so precisely that determination could be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it would be -- it would be our -- well, first of all, we support the Court's approach, and it's -- we would be more than happy to provide the Court with all materials necessary to make the most objective finding, whether it is perceived to support the expert's opinion or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when any issue comes up like that, we urge the Court to take a look at the underlying materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we have to find a fair balance between finding objective support and -- and sometimes it's just too much. I mean, I take it there are at least 10.000 witnesses in the -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina who could tell us something which might have some relevance for the case, and nevertheless we can't hear 10.000 witnesses. Then, Mr. Stewart, is there anything you would like to say in this respect or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's really a question, with respect, Your Honour. Well, first of all, I'm just wondering what the time scale was that the Court had in mind in relation to this -- this Nielsen exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider -- we are now informed about what is available and what is not available, and we have not yet considered any time scale at this moment, so the Chamber would further now see whether it will seek further access to these materials and in what way to seek that access.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just make this remark for the Court's consideration in looking at the time scale, that it's not difficult to see the attractions from the Trial Chamber's point of view in narrowing down the material for consideration; on the other hand, I hope it's not difficult for the Trial Chamber to see the negative impact for the Defence of finding the time and the resources to do what must necessarily be a very time-consuming exercise - potentially, anyway -- to try to identify such a limited amount of material to make these points. Those are simply concerns to express now and to invite the Trial Chamber, please, to have those in mind in considering the nature of the exercise and the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can imagine that if this would be a problem, to say, let's make a random selection and see whether this type of report are of any relevance at all. That's another way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, a random selection can be done by the Trial Chamber, with respect, Your Honour. If it's going to be random, that can be done by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. I just said that -- I said: If this would be a problem, that is the time-consumption, and I then presented an alternative way of dealing with this material, that is to make a random selection. So you only confirm what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm delighted to be able to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was a response to your concerns about consumption of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just with respect to the consumption of time, I think the most burdensome aspect of that, and most time-consuming aspect of that is largely completed. It's not something we would ask the Defence to duplicate on its on, so the materials we have assembled would obviously be made available to them, and that should at least reduce one aspect of the -- of any project involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nevertheless, reading and selecting would take considerable time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand. I wanted to make a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We also note the Prosecution -- we have a large measure of cooperation, friendly cooperation on all these things, and I appreciate the help, but we must, with respect, always remember we are on opposite sides of the case and, therefore, material we are presented with by the Prosecution may necessarily require considerable investigation of -- work by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence has asked in some respects guidance on the -- in relation to the omnibus order. We are preparing to give a response to that. There are a few matters. I do understand that the visa problem, as far as Mr. Lakic is concerned, has been resolved. Then there is a fair chance that despite the order the Chamber issued yesterday, there's a fair chance that Mr. Bjelica could not be brought to The Hague by the 21st of March. The Chamber would very much like the Defence to give quite some thought on a back-up plan if Mr. Bjelica would not arrive in time. I think he was announced in October or November as -- to be one of the witnesses. In December he was detained, from what I understand, which means that the problem of getting him here in time has been known for quite some time. I think even the Chamber has drawn the attention to it at a certain moment. So if we don't -- we don't get him here by the 21st of March, at least the Defence is invited to make a back-up plan. Then there's one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to those two points on information? First of all, Mr. Lakic, we understand, have no reason to believe that he's not actually on his way here today. So the visa problem has been solved. As far as we know, he's actually arriving this evening. So far as Mr. Bjelica is concerned, yes, the back-up plan has been noted and we are working on that. And, Your Honour, as soon as this particular bit of today's case is concerned, I hope Your Honours will forgive me if I walk out in front of Your Honours because I have a meeting straight away on the subject of Mr. Bjelica with the Victims and Witnesses Section to follow that up as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, once that happens, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's one problem with a -- well, at least keep it short because there's no pseudonym granted yet, but with the possibility that a protected witness would not be fit to travel to The Hague, as far as we understood. The question is whether the Defence has considered asking for videolink testimony in respect of this witness, because preparing for videolink takes some time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can answer that. Your Honour, the Defence has considered and does consider the whole range of possibilities, and specifically in relation to that witness; however, step number one is -- well, we are pressing for a medical certificate and of course we wish to assess whether, when that arrives, it provides any basis whatever for exploring actively that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would the Prosecution insist on the medical report? Would the Prosecution otherwise oppose against a videolink testimony of this protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I pre-empt that? The Defence is insisting on the medical report as step number one, Your Honour, because we will make no such application unless there is sufficient basis in the medical information to support such an application. So the Prosecution -- of course, the question -- perfectly fair to address to the Prosecution, but Your Honour should understand, please, where the matter starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes one even accepts a medical condition without a supporting report. If there's any dispute about the medical condition, then usually in this dispute the medical reports are necessary. So if there's any doubt on the Defence side whether there is a medical condition which would prevent the witness to travel to The Hague, of course I can imagine that you would like to know for sure whether the witness really is unable to travel and perhaps otherwise ask for a subpoena or something like that. But I was just trying to be practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, absolutely. We accept that entirely. The reason I had used the phrase "medical information," that was carefully chosen because we're not sticklers for certificates if we are satisfied. But, Your Honour, there is another matter, apart from anything else involved in the videolink suggestion, which is the disruption and difficulty for the Defence in calling this witness without a -- without that witness coming to The Hague, Your Honour, is potentially significant. The Defence has very little enthusiasm for that step, given the practical consequences for us in preparing the witness. Perhaps I can just leave it there, Your Honour, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then there's another matter of Witness Maricic. We'll deal with that at a later stage. We need a bit more time to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, may I, Your Honour? I apologise for jumping up and down, Your Honour, but of course, like Your Honour, I'm trying as well to cooperate in dealing with as many of these really quite considerable practical matters as quickly as possible. So far as Mr. Maricic is concerned, Your Honour, we are -- as we get into this week, we are running quickly into the difficulty. He is due to arrive on Saturday night; that I can tell Your Honour. He will arrive on Saturday -- it was on Saturday; I'm not sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was on my mind, Mr. Stewart, to deal with it still today but a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's perfectly -- I shall be -- well, I shall be available. Mr. Josse is here, Your Honour, thank you for that. If it is today, then I sit down straight away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else? If not, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had e-mailed Mr. Zahar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the fact I needed to raise scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It really runs into exactly what has just been discussed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic is arriving, we hope, in the early part of this evening. Realistically, I will not be in a position to call him tomorrow afternoon. The only period of time between his arrival and tomorrow afternoon that I have at my disposal to see him is, quite obviously, tomorrow morning; and that, simply, is not enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How about Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thursday afternoon I will be in a position to call him. I can't ask for more time than that, but a day and a half, with respect, is reasonable and it will allow me to take him to see Mr. Krajisnik, which we've done with every -- or virtually every witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to consider that during one of the next breaks and we'll inform you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I mean, apart from consequential arrangements for the Chamber and its staff, there are obviously consequential arrangements for us; for example, the relevant prison appointment, that type of thing. The sooner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're trying to do -- as you may have noticed, your Rule 90 bis request, we invited the Prosecution to respond orally and to deliver a decision right away and they are dealing with these matters as all being urgent in a similar way, but at the same time we sometimes -- you would appreciate that we now and then want our own five minutes at least for thinking --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course I understand. Could I -- just for the avoidance of any doubt, in effect I'm asking the Court not to sit tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Half a word sometimes is enough for this Chamber, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the only matter. We do need to return to the subject of Mr. Maricic later today, as Mr. Stewart indicated. That's almost as urgent, not quite as urgent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with that. It's at the top of our priority list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojko. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I believe the bundles have been distributed, but -- I'm sure the witness has the bundle, yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please -- Mr. Radojko, the Prosecution does -- at least, what often happens, he'll put some questions to you in relation to documents. He'll indicate usually under what tab you'll find the documents he'll ask questions about. Please consult only those documents once requested to do so by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Radojko.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to move through this part of your testimony as quickly and efficiently as possible. I think we will be aided considerably by the fact that you have both given an interview before and, more importantly I think, have testified before a Trial Chamber with regard to many of these matters, and I will be referring as much as possible to your previous comments so that we don't have to go through elaborations on those again, and of course I will make it clear to you when I am doing so. First matter I'd like to touch upon, Mr. Radojko, is the matter of the SDS. You testified before the Brdjanin Court in June -- or July of 2003 that the general principle was that if the Main Board issued instructions to the Municipal Board, the Municipal Board was obliged to carry them out unless, for some reason, that was impossible. Correct? And that can be found at page 20028 of the testimony. That's correct, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I don't think I need to read that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and let me point out that both the Chamber and Mr. Josse from the Defence have copies of the documents, the testimony, and the interview to the extent I'll be referring to them. And if I misquote them, I trust the -- that will be brought to my attention, but I will obviously endeavour to read them as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are aware that they're not in evidence, but you just use them for us because I -- after our discussions, I took care that -- they are beyond my reach and -- although it might be that there are still some copies around --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I too want to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did speak to Mr. Tieger prior to Your Honours coming in and said I was going to raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I took it that Mr. Tieger will refer to it, so just to have a basis that we would only, if the witness would say: No, that's not what I testified, or My testimony is misunderstood, or anything else, that we would then look at the specific portion if Mr. Tieger wanted to raise the issue of inconsistency in earlier testimony and present testimony or a statement in the usual way, but that this reference is just I would say instrumental in getting quickly to the testimony of the witness rather than anything else. Is that a correct understanding, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's exactly what my submission would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then. Everyone agrees. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, just moving on from the principle that the Municipal Boards were obliged to carry out those instructions. You also explained during the course of your interview with the OTP that instructions from the Main Board to Municipal Boards were usually conveyed orally. Whoever went to Pale would receive instructions. That was at page 26. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in principle. That's the state of affairs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You explained further there were also written instructions, and indeed it was one of your jobs to compile comments and proposals for the Municipal Board or Regional Board of the SDS that resulted from meetings. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that applied to this one specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at one of those written instructions, and if you could turn, please, to tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I believe that -- I don't think that -- I think that's P90, tab 8; P529, tab 51 already in evidence. That's the first meeting of the party secretariat of Bosanski Petrovac on December 26th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph of that document, sir, do we see the members of the party secretariat listed, either present or absent?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn your attention to item 2. Item 2 states: "The instruction on the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency circumstances needs to be typed in seven copies and every member of the Secretariat is to be given a copy." Now, first of all, sir, that's a reference to the document that you saw yesterday, the so-called Variant A and B document, the instructions of December 19th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as the minutes indicate, every member was to be given a copy of the document that was typed seven times for that purpose. You were asked during the course of your testimony in Brdjanin whether you were given a copy, and you said: "I don't remember that, but quite possibly. I suppose I was." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that, and that's why I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were also asked if the instructions were discussed, and you said: "According to the minutes, I believe so, but it was a long time ago. But yes, that is how it should have been in the regular course of business." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also explained in the course of your interview on a couple of occasions that the document appeared authentic to you from the -- that: "The content would correspond to the atmosphere and events at the time, and from the content I believe this to be an authentic document for the time." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about implementation of the document yesterday, and when you were asked about that in the Brdjanin case, you said at page 20045 that item 1 with respect to regular standing duties was implemented for a while and later ceased. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That you didn't have daily meetings of the secretariat, which is item 2, because it wasn't technically feasible, but that you did meet when necessary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not a fair summary of the answer, in my submission, at page 20045. My learned friend left out: "And there was no need for that."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I appreciate that, and I'm -- apologise for the inadvertent omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to item 3, forming a Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would you like to have this specifically put to the witness or is it now agreed upon that this was part of his statement and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to forming a Crisis Staff, I believe you indicated that that was not necessary because a Crisis Staff had been formed earlier, on October 24th in 1991. And you indicated that that staff must have been formed following the SDS instructions that we saw in that earlier document. And to remind you, the earlier document -- the earlier documents that were shown to you were the telex from Mr. Brdjanin referring to a meeting in Sarajevo with Dr. Karadzic on October 26th, 1991, and the state of emergency imposed by Dr. Karadzic on October 18th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that this was the case. I accept it, although I cannot remember the details of it. This was taking place among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also indicated in your interview that with respect to item number 9, cancellation of leave, that instruction was rigorously implemented. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to annual leave, that's correct. Annual leave could not be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then I believe you indicated - and I'll try to sum it up; I believe this is accurate, you can tell me otherwise - that with respect to the other items listed in the instructions, that they were deemed either unnecessary or not relevant to Petrovac, which was a Variant A municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as you know, the instructions of December 19th are broken down in two ways. First, with respect to municipalities, the A and B municipalities, the majority or minority Serbian municipalities; and second, with respect to two levels or stages, a first and a second. Let me -- before I ask you any questions about that, let me ask you about your diary or notebook that you prepared in 1992. During the course of 1992, you took notes by hand in a notebook that you have subsequently had a chance to see and review. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did take the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that notebook stayed in your desk in the municipal building when you left Petrovac in 1995. You had an opportunity to review that before you testified in the Brdjanin case, and you confirmed its authenticity and accuracy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about one -- among the questions asked about your diary during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case, you were asked about a diary entry on -- for February 14th, 1992, and that portion of the diary was shown to you and was read out loud. That can be found at page 20049. You were asked to read it out and did so, and you said: "I will read it out aloud and I can also interpret it." And you read it: "Activate the second degree, activate organs of authority so that they practically carry out their duties." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything what I said still stands. My statement went as far as my memory served me, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was the quote that appeared in your diary on February 14th -- well, let me ask you first before I go on: You went on to explain what that reference -- what that quote referred to, and you said: "With -- by 'activating the second degree,' what they mean is according to what I recollect from the instructions on the division of the municipalities into the A and B categories, I think the second degree or level is a higher level of alert and readiness, and 'to activate the organs of authority to practically carry out their duties,' this probably refers to the group of the B type where the Serbs did not have a majority so these organs of theirs, which had separated, needed to actually function and perform as an administration or an administrative service for the citizens because up until that point they were just formally organised." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you attended a meeting in Sarajevo in 1992 for Dr. Novakovic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Novakovic, yes, but that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the activation of the second degree reflected in your diary on 14 February, that is the activation of the, in particular, B-type municipalities where the Serbs did not have a majority, was a reference to the speech by Dr. Karadzic on February 14th, increasing the level of the 19 December instructions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I cannot really say at this time. I -- that's as far as the group B municipalities are concerned. I am more familiar with group A municipalities because that was where the situation more or less remained as it was. I know that there was more discussion of the B-type municipalities, as they are called in the instructions, where the population is mixed and where the Serb population was separated from others and formed their own municipality. That's at least my understanding of it. That was the case, for instance, with the neighbouring municipalities of Bihac and Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I -- we're now talking about what appears at least on the list as a potential exhibit. Are you going to tender the diary or portions of it? It's tab 4. It looks, at least -- that's what I find on my list, diary of Jovo Radojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I will be tendering the diary, Your Honour, but I -- my understanding was that it was in evidence. Probably more prudent for me to check at the break whether or not my understanding was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it's not, as such, indicated on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll resolve that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you want us to look at it anyhow, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to look at anything yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, activating the second degree is the first reference in your diary of that date, but there are other references to what was said at the meeting you attended. The second one is a reference to the referendum. "The Serbs must not take part in it in view of the fact that they have already given their declaration on that matter." And in that connection, let me turn your attention and the Court's attention to a telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and President Novakovic on February 7th, 1992. And that is P64A, and that's tab 14, sir. Let me just draw your attention to one quick reference found on the -- toward the bottom of the first page. As you can see from the beginning, president of the municipality, Novakovic, wishes to speak to Dr. Karadzic. And then the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm sorry to interrupt you again. I see that on your list it's P64A at tab 25. Is there any confusion or is P64A maybe a -- let me just look at P64 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because ... P64A is 28 binders. Perhaps both of them are from P64A and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry that I don't have the available tab number, however I also note that -- well, again, we can -- I can check this -- we can give it a provisional number or we can address that when this issue is more clearly resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you would find the binder and the tab number, then we could identify this whether it has got a number yet or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I was just drawing your attention to that portion of the telephone conversation where Mr. Novakovic says: "So, President Karadzic, it's like this. There's a couple of things I need to consult you about. First of all, regarding the Referendum." And then they continue, as you can see, on page 2. Mr. Novakovic, after some discussion about information he's received, says: "I'd like to know, as a member of the Main Board ..." And Dr. Karadzic says: "We'll have a meeting of the Main Board, I can't tell you anything over the phone." Mr. Novakovic says: "I know." Dr. Karadzic says: "Nothing." Mr. Novakovic says: "So, views will be taken on this." Dr. Karadzic says: "Yes." Mr. Novakovic says: "We shall not be taking any actions by then." Dr. Karadzic says: "Don't take any, don't do anything before the Main Board meeting." Mr. Novakovic says: "Yes, yes." And Dr. Karadzic says: "The Main Board and presidents of all Municipal Boards will attend." Now, as you can see from your own notes of February 14th, Mr. Radojko, the issue of the referendum was indeed addressed on that occasion, indicating: "The Serbs must not take part in it in view of the fact that they have already given their declaration on this matter." The Court has the speech by Dr. Karadzic in evidence and can identify the passages more fully, but does that refresh your recollection that the meeting which you attended for Mr. Novakovic was the meeting that addressed both the referendum that was discussed in this telephone conversation and the activation of level two of the instructions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember having gone to a meeting on behalf of the leading persons who were absent in order to collect information. This is the first time I see this conversation. I didn't know it was intercepted, and I didn't know that Karadzic was still an active physician at the time. My impression wasn't that this had to do with the referendum. I was attending a meeting when the Republika Srpska was declared. That was when the Serb MPs walked out of the Assembly. That might have taken place after the referendum, although I'm not sure. This visit of mine did not ask for any active participation; that's why I don't remember it that much. This particular meeting was held on the 14th, and if you take a look at the minutes, probably you'll see that I was keeping the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my notes say that I was somewhere on the 14th, then that must be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- let me -- I want to move on from there, but let me, just for the benefit of the Court in particular, note that the -- the additional references in your diary taken on that occasion. We've already noted the activation of level two, the reference to the referendum. You also say: "None of our people in the commissions and the lists should be drawn up on the basis of reciprocity."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note for the Court that in the speech by Dr. Karadzic in evidence. You can find that reference in page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also note: "Courtesy toward the monitors ... "Do not instruct the referendum, it is the right of every people. "The alienation of power on the part of the party impermissible. "The strategic goal: To uphold Serbia and Montenegro, a necessary support for our goals. "We do not recognise any sort of control as far as the referendum is concerned. "Definition of the Serb people ... "And problems of the functional connecting and putting authority into operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those references, for the benefit of the Court, Your Honour, may be found respectively at pages 9, 8, 11, 12 through 13, 21, 23, and 22 of the speech that is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, let me turn next to the Petrovac municipality and the situation and events there in late 1991 and 1992. First of all, I'd like to -- I'd like to indicate to you a decision by the ARK Crisis Staff, with which I believe you're familiar, and that is the decision of May 4th, 1992, decision that general public mobilisation is ordered on the entire territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is P64A, Your Honour, and that is contained in the series of the ARK Gazette which was discussed both during the course of the Treanor testimony and the during the course of the testimony by Mr. Vasic, for example. There may have been other references to those documents during the course of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That decision, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What tab are we at this moment talking about, Mr. -- 64A is, I think, 200 documents or something like that, if not 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be another matter that I'll have to provide the -- give more specificity to the Court for. We'll try to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And where do we find it now, in which tab in our present material?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's found in 25, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I referred to 25 before, yes, that's true. That's an Official Gazette, Banja Luka, 5th of June, 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That decision was taken pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just see. Did you find it, Mr. Radojko, tab 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Keeping that in mind, I'd like you to turn to tab 52, please, which is a report dated May 10th, 1992, by Dr. Novakovic in his capacity as president of the National Security Council for Petrovac. And that's the report on the conduct of mobilisation in Bosanski Petrovac municipality. And Mr. Novakovic indicates that: "Further to your letter of May 8th, we hereby inform you that the general mobilisation of men liable for military service and of listed material and technical resources was conducted in the territory of Bosanski Petrovac Municipality as soon as it was declared." It goes on to talk about -- it mentions that: "Most of the conscripts were mobilised before the declaration of general mobilisation under a special plan by unit commanders so that the rest of the military-age men were mobilised without major problems. "Muslim men of military age did not respond to the general mobilisation except in individual cases." And I believe you were asked some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, this document needs a number. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 52 [Realtime transcript read in error "32"] Your Honours, would be P1098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe you were asked about this matter during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case, and you indicated that mobilisation had taken place in large measure before the order and that, in addition, Muslims, for the most part, did not respond. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The mobilisation had basically been fully completed before this. The authorities which existed at the time carried it out, and it was still the JNA which was in charge in the former Yugoslavia. And this was only sent as an expression of the formal acceptance of those orders and requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And similarly, turning to tab 19, which reflect the minutes of the 17th meeting of the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff held on 24 May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, I see tab 32 would need a number, but on your list, tab 32 has P748, tab 4 -- oh, 52. Then it appears not correctly in the transcript. 52 would be 1098. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I was saying, Mr. Radojko, similarly the minutes of that meeting in item 1 reflect President Novakovic reading out the order concerning the general mobilisation in the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and making introductory remarks in that respect, again with Mr. Miljevic indicating that the mobilisation was essentially completed before the order and that Bosanski Petrovac was a bit ahead. Correct? Just looking at the item, item 1, and then the quick remarks by Mr. Miljevic.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. There's no need for me to look at it because it is fully in line with my memory of the facts. I can see that. I can see that it tallies fully. So the mobilisation had been finished. What it is about here is that those who had received the call for mobilisation must be made to respond to that call in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you, as I indicated before, also were asked questions about this during the course of your testimony in Brdjanin, and you testified at page 20040 that by December 1991, in fact, there was a huge increase in the number of men mobilised, although they were mobilised and then those ranks were filled as the weeks progressed. Is that right? Perhaps it would -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I haven't quite understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to have been a problem with my headset.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to look quickly at tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 10 would need a number, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just double-check that, if I may. Sorry, Your Honour, that would be tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 9. Would that need a number? No number appears on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 9 would be P1099, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's tab 9, and you said tab 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, tab 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but tab 19 has not received a number yet. It's the 17th meeting

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 19, Your Honour, would be P1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking quickly at tab 9, you see the reference at the bottom of the long paragraph before the list of material supplies that: "The reorganisation of the Bosanski Petrovac Territorial Defence has increased the numerical strength of the TO forces from 540 conscripts to 1.700 conscripts." And then it lists the material supplies sought and you -- as I believe you indicated in your testimony in the Brdjanin case, indeed, in December 1991, there was a huge increase in the number of men mobilised. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there must have been a misunderstanding here. I do understand. I believe that there was an increase, not a decrease, of conscripts. It says that instead of 240, it was 1.700. So there was the overall population of between 11 and 12.000 people, and there should have been a battalion. That was the general assessment, that a battalion could be formed on the basis of that number of inhabits. Now, due to war, they changed their plans and brought this figure up to 1.700. And so if we think in terms of 5.400 people who could join the army, it would be slightly more than half the population, so it wouldn't have been possible. It is simply that the number of possible conscripts was increased by authorising the mobilisation of people that could not normally be mobilised. So people were mobilised not on the basis of the actual possibilities, but on the basis of their needs, of what would seem to be the need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a question. Could we ask the witness if he could tell us in a few words what the situation was like in December 1991 in Bosanski Petrovac, why there was such a situation that there was a need in the increase in conscripts. What happened at the moment? Because this is what I'm reading in this request: [In English] "In view of the political and security situation in Yugoslavia and the military conflict provoked by fascistoid forces on the territory of Bosanski Petrovac municipality ..." [Interpretation] Could you please tell us what happened exactly at that moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember, Your Honour. It is the period in which the former Yugoslavia still existed, the state of former Yugoslavia still existed. And since in Slovenia and in Croatia at that time, as far as I can remember, the secession had already been proclaimed and those countries were recognised as separate states, the units were withdrawing to the part of the territory still under the control of the JNA, and they took the equipment as well. Since JNA didn't have enough conscripts from the rest of the country, they changed their organisation plans. And so I remember that the Knin command - and I think this was first a division and then it was turned into a corps - it gained new significance, as it were, and their plan of recruitment encompassed our territory as well, reached very far into our territory, because their borders of the military zones or regions in the past did not tally with the geographical or political borders of the republics and regions in a civilian sense. And so that's why their units were filled from the ranks of our population. It is for this reason that this commander here, Vrzina, who was a kind of TO commander, so units which would be stationed and recruited from our local territory and who would not be, so to say, the first class, the top class, of military units. So, yes, that's how these numbers increased. They were on the increase. They were not decreasing by any means. That's what I wanted to emphasise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just touching quickly on one other subject, you also testified in the Brdjanin case at pages 20061 and 20062 that by and large the Muslims did not respond. The number of Muslims who responded was insignificant and it was a bone of contention that Muslims refused mobilisation calls. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that some small numbers of Muslims responded, but I don't really know what the reason was. Actually, they did not respond in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm not asking you for the reason, but thanks. I'm trying to move through as quickly as I can. I appreciate that, but we'll try to move forward from question to question. Now, you spoke about the situation in Petrovac further in your testimony in Brdjanin, and you indicated that there were no armed conflicts between Muslims and Serbs in Petrovac. "There was no such thing in our area," at pages 20099, 20, through 20100. That Muslims in Petrovac, in your view, did not pose a serious threat, at page 20069. That: "Because of the actual numbers involved and the actual relations involved, we never thought that we were jeopardised in any way by Muslims, at least not those from the area of our municipality," at 20125. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Some -- well, there was some minor reasons, but they're not of any significance. Only at one point things were different, but for the most part it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you also discussed the issue of disarming and weapons seizures or collections in your testimony in Brdjanin. At pages 20077 through 78, you were shown during the course of that testimony the same 4th of May document that you had a chance to look at here in court with respect to the mobilisation and which also indicated that: "All paramilitary formations and individuals who had illegally possessed weapons and ammunition are to immediately, and by 1500 hours on the 11th of May, at the latest, surrender them to the municipal authorities." You were shown the document from the same Gazette of 11 May 1992, another order by the ARK Crisis Staff, extending the deadline for surrender of illegally acquired weapons to the 14th of May. And you testified in the Brdjanin case that you were aware that there were orders for disarming and deadlines. "Yes," you said, "there were orders of that type and also I heard it raised in discussions. So there were deadlines for disarmament and I know that they were extended." That's correct, isn't it? You were aware of those ARK orders and the extension of the deadlines?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've talked about the ARK orders, but I know that those calls had been repeated on a number of occasions. About the weapons, I mean. And if I made a note of the ARK order, then I must have known about it. I can't recall whether it was a strict procedure, fully in line with that order, or whether there was a local reason to act like that. Both are possible, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the Petrovac Crisis Staff undertook actions to disarm so-called paramilitary formations and citizens, and I would ask you to look at tab 20, and in particular, decision number 4 on page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, which provides that: "In the area of the Petrovac municipality, the disarmament of paramilitary formations and citizens who illegally possess weapons will start on the 24th of May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, tab 20 is P90, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, your diary on May 9th, Mr. Radojko, addresses the issue of weapons and indicates the type of weapons that were at issue. And you also testified about that during the course of your testimony in Brdjanin. So you were asked what kind of weapons were sought -- what kind of weapons did the Muslims have and what kind of weapons were sought by the disarming efforts in the Petrovac municipality. And at 20062 you said, indicating it could mean two things. "One, and perhaps more likely one, is that it deals with the legal weapons owned by Muslims, because there were hunters, sportsmen and the like, mostly as hunters. Or to protect their property. So those would be mostly pistols or revolvers, so I guess it is that kind of weapon that is meant here. And possibly, also, the Muslims had managed to come by some of the formation, some of the proper army weapons, and perhaps any weapons owned by Muslims are meant here." And you also spoke about that at 20083 of the Brdjanin testimony. And you were asked again about the disarming of Muslims in the Petrovac municipality. And you were asked at the end of a long question referring to a report which you'll have a chance to see during the course of your testimony today, a report by the SJB on its activities, you were asked: "In reality, were the people being disarmed the non-Serb population?" And you said: "Well, I think judging by the circumstances, I do think that it was the non-Serbs who were disarmed by and large. Possibly that some of this weaponry, especially the army weaponry, were also seized from Serbs who were involved in excesses, but the hunting weapons, at least as far as I know about that time, they were mostly -- such weaponry was mostly seized from Muslims, and as a rule, their hunting weapons were licensed. They all had their licences for such weapons." And you indicated further on page 2084 [sic] that among the reasons you were aware of this is because daily -- almost daily reports were submitted by the police regarding their operations relative to what went on on the ground. That's all correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, with the proviso that I think I'd explained about those other weapons that'd been taken away. You see, I found about those details at meetings, and the police would submit reports on those occasions, that's correct. But the other bit that's missing is that other weapons had been found there that were combat weapons that had been supplied illegally and hidden. And the police found it at that formation and probably when that decision needed to be made, they already had some indication and they needed some -- something to corroborate their action. I suppose if we were to compare their reports about the actual army weapons taken from Muslims, we would see clearly whether this preceded this action or not. In case it did, it would probably be one way of justifying their action, from their point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger - but I'm also addressing the witness - are there any such reports? I mean comparing reports, if we haven't seen them, is a bit difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what the Prosecution has, but since I was in charge of all the archives in that municipality back then, I know for a fact that police officers would submit reports almost on a daily basis following requests from the Crisis Staff, reports about robberies, et cetera, and they asked for these reports because they felt that that could go some way to answer dissipating dissatisfaction with the work of the police, and people who had been robbed would submit lists to the Prosecutor's office. The Prosecutor's office never did anything about it, but they put everything on file for future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, you were talking about report -- reports about the actual army weapons taken from Muslims. Are there any reports which would support your evidence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are such reports because the weapons that were taken from them were either the weapons from the army that had been hidden and also the ones that they had licenses for. And for the most part they themselves brought those weapons to the police station and all that was documented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did they have to give the weapons they had licenses for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know that. As far as I know, the police invited them to surrender the weapons for safety reasons, as they put it. There was the pressure exerted by the Serb population because of the Muslims refused to respond to call-ups. The Serb men were concerned about the Muslims still around the town, and they were afraid that the Muslims would break into the arms depots that was scattered around the town that contained great quantities of weapons belonging to the former army and that they might use them against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say -- I don't know whether we are talking about approximately the same time, but you said: The police could not protect the Muslims against gangs that were around. And at the same time you say: Weapons were taken from them because it's -- it was too dangerous for the Serbs. I'm trying to reconcile the two considerations. At the one hand take even licensed arms from them and then say: You better -- it's -- we can't protect you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour; however, at the time when the people still had their weapons, they did not dare use them. There were cases where the Muslims received official weapons from the police to use for their own safety but they did not dare to use them. They did not dare to use them even earlier on. There were cases when they called on their friends, Serbs, to come and help them defend themselves from these gangs appearing at their doorstep, trying to rob them. It would place them in a highly unfavourable position to use weapons in their defence against such criminals because this would have negative reverberations in the public eye, and they were very much aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I still have some difficulties in seeing the logic of it all. You say: We had to take their weapons because otherwise they would have used these weapons to get more weapons, whereas at the same time you say: They did not even dare to use the weapons they had, and even if they were provided with other weapons, they would ask the Serbs to come and help them. So they couldn't use those weapons. And if you say that it -- it would have negative reverberations in the public eye if they would have used weapons against such criminals, then I'm asking myself whether being in an unprotected situation and having to leave, for that reason, the municipality, whether that would be the smaller or the larger disadvantage in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only make assessments of that situation here, Your Honour. I was not charged with dealing with these situations at the time. I believe that the members of the Crisis Staff and the police administration made choices as to what the best course of action was. It is true that some of the Muslims got hold of army weapons. Whether this had been done with the support of the police or not, I don't know, but I know that in the subsequent disarmament campaign, the weapons were found. I know that there is a lack of logic that is inherent in these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radojko -- while the last part of your answer was related to my question, some of the other parts were not. And then could you please explain why you'd be looked at in a negative way if you would protect yourself against criminal gangs. It would place them, as you said, in a highly unfavourable position to use weapons in their defence against such criminals because this would have negative reverberations in the public eye. So the public eye, if someone would defend himself against criminals, would be -- say that is to be negative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, no, but under those specific circumstances, yes. And I believe that every single of those Muslims would confirm what I'm saying. Nobody would admit to the fact that they had appeared at someone's doorstep in order to rob them. Let's say a person thus defending his own property ends up shooting someone. The one's who's been shot will not say: Well, I was there in order to rob the person. We simply stopped by to get a glass of water and he started shooting at us Serbs. And you know, by the time you actually manage to explain what had happened under the general chaos that was prevailing, it would be too late. I was there; I know what the general feeling was. Only those who had good friends and were better off were in a better position. I know, for instance, Mr. Latinovic. His brother went to protect a good friend of his, a Muslim, because this Muslim was accosted by a group of people who asked for money from him. The Muslim said that he did not have cash ready-made, and these people returned, the gang returned, asking for money. When the door was opened by this Serb, they said: Oh, we've made a mistake. We've appeared at the wrong doorstep. And had this person gone about this whole affair in a different way, seeking justice, God knows what the outcome would be, and that was the difficult situation. The atmosphere that prevailed at the time was such that the people simply were divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your example tells me that it was relatively easy to stop the criminals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, they gave up the whole idea because they realised that the Muslim had a friend who was a Serb and who was holding a good position. That's why they gave it up. And they knew that if they killed the man, then they would have been prosecuted. For instance, Mr. Sepak, who was a TO commander for a period of time, appeared desperate one morning. This was at the time when the people were actually forced to leave. He told us that when people were passing around the town, there were others hiding in shadows of the corners, addressing threats to them. And that's why the people were afraid to use weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for that reason you thought they were better off without?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any particular opinion about that. I knew that the weapons were collected from reports. That was at the time when the police came to submit a report to the president. That was when I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I used the word "you," I did not specifically mention you as a person but those who were responsible for that course of action. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger -- oh, I'm looking at the clock and I think you should not proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour's observation there needs to be put to the witness, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What observation do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The very last one. If Your Honour is going to make, with respect, an observation like that about what Your Honour meant, the witness needs to be entitled to deal with it; that "you" didn't refer to him, "you" referred to the authorities in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I said, "And for that reason you thought ..." I had in mind -- but if the witness wants to respond to that, those he -- he's told us ordered or thought it better to take the -- even the licensed weapons from Muslims that possessed them. But if the witness would like to further comment on that, I will give him an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said at a certain moment, but by "you" I was rather referring to those responsible for -- for taking that course of action. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my understanding of it. In fact, as far as the taking of the weapons is concerned, that was merely my opinion, what -- whether that was positive or not. I did not have this information at the time. I'm merely thinking about what the reason for taking these weapons away might have been. I was trying to make a logical inference and perhaps I made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll continue at 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I could give you information on the two matters that were urgent. If I do it now, I do it in the presence of the witness. There's no need -- I mean, it's not dramatic but I prefer to do it in the absence of the witness. But if you would say: No, having it now instead of one hour later will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It will make a difference, Your Honour, for logistical arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What -- I think whether or not we will sit tomorrow, we - and that's not exactly the same question - we'll allow you to start the examination-in-chief of your next witness on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not the same as not sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the other matter about witness -- I think he's not protected, Mr. Maricic, that's a matter -- would that make any difference whether I tell you now or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, that would make no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll leave that for later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, the Court inquired about reports with respect to disarming of Muslims. Perhaps I could ask you to turn to page 39. That's a report to the Assembly of the Bosnia -- of Bosanski Petrovac. You had an opportunity to see that during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case. The report indicates in part, in paragraph 2, that the public security station has borne the brunt of the task of disarming paramilitary formations, and describes how it completely broke up the SDA, took a series of plans and organised operational measures to cover the areas where paramilitary formations were based, searching their apartments and surroundings, detaining persons who possessed illegal types of long-barrelled fire-arms, isolating persons who had demonstrated extremist views with respect to the policies of the Serbian people, et cetera. And then it contains a list of items seized, including -- and breaking them down into legal and illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I believe that needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue on the arming, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to ask one additional question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand why Mr. Tieger's done that, but if that's going to be done in the course of a cross-examination, then in my submission, the witness should be entitled to deal with the assertion made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I thought, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Tieger asked for a number and that I then intervened before he could put a question to the witness. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In which case I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, good to hear that, Mr. Josse. But I'd like to ask one question. Mr. Radojko, at an earlier stage we looked at a list of weapons which would be needed for the 1.700 men rather than the 450. That was a request, I think for TO, and it was about a broader mobilisation of TO. Was there -- were there, among these 1.700, was this a TO composed of Serbs or was it a mixed composition at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to locate this. Let me just look at the date. All the way through to the departure -- through to the point when the Muslim population left, in the TO and the army there were Muslims. Some of the Muslims even left the area together with the Serb population as late as in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Out of these 1.700, how many, approximately, would be non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. But judging from what I know, there weren't many at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were not many. Yes. Then, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, as I indicated, you had an opportunity when you were presented with this document during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case, at pages 20082 to 83, you indicated that because you were the secretary of the Executive Board, this was not a document that would have been directed to you in terms of the regular procedure. But what you can say is that "I know --" well, I'll quote you: "What I can say is that I know from other sources that weapons of similar type were being seized. Those were mostly hunting weapons and some of the army weapons were also found." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. However, according to this report of the Assembly - I have a very poor copy - but I believe most of the weapons there were hunting weapons and army weapons constituted only a small percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, earlier, Mr. Radojko, we looked at some of the ARK Crisis Staff directives --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you kindly speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- including, I believe, the one from May 11th which extended the deadline for surrender of illegally acquired weapons. That same session of the Crisis Staff, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, also reached a conclusion that management posts in Krajina enterprises must be filled by persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This Court has also seen other conclusions by the ARK Crisis Staff in that connection, and I believe you were also given an opportunity during the course in the Brdjanin case to look at some of those conclusions. On page 20132 there was a discussion about the conclusions of 11 May, which I just indicated; 13 May 1992, which provides that the "management posts in enterprises must be filled absolutely by persons loyal to the Serbian Republic" of Bosnia and Herzegovina; 26th May, "leading posts in social and public organisations may be occupied only by the most professional cadres who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian people in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And you indicated on page 20133 that you were familiar with the contents of that decision. It said: "... that there was such a decision and I suppose that the army command is requesting it in this relation." Then you were asked -- then you referred specifically to a dismissal of somebody whom you had met who was very upset about the whole thing. And the question was asked: "In fact, dismissals of non-Serbs were taking place, weren't they, in Petrovac? Whatever you personally felt about it." And you responded: "Yes, they were taking place."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think my learned friend should add they resisted it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. The entire passage: "Yes, I was familiar with the contents of that decision, that there was such a decision and I suppose that the army command is requesting it in this relation. We resisted [Realtime transcript read in error "requested"] it for a very long time but eventually this man was dismissed and I met him after that and he was very cut up about the whole thing." Is that correct, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, let me just see. Now I do not find the part, but Mr. Tieger quotes the whole of it. The portion you read does not appear, at least not on the transcript. Mr. Tieger, would you please read the entire passage, including the portion Mr. Josse referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I just did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the words spoken by Mr. Josse do not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason is because I slightly misquoted them, in fairness. The words were: "We resisted it for a very long time." I'm afraid even when Mr. Tieger re-read it, it is incorrect in the transcript, I notice, again. So I think Mr. Tieger should do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read it again so we know exactly what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. "But yes, I was familiar with the contents of that decision, that there was such a decision and I suppose that the army command is requesting it in this relation. We resisted it for a very long time but eventually this man was dismissed and I met him after that and he was very cut up about the whole thing." And then I went on: "In fact, dismissals --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now it's clear to everyone. And then you put a question to the witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I need just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question was, Your Honour: "Is that correct, Mr. Radojko?" I assume Mr. Tieger is going to ask Mr. Radojko about the passage again in those terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that Mr. Tieger is reorganising himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we've finished that passage. Please, Mr. Radojko, if you will respond to that one question.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, I was asked whether I met the man who was dismissed because of his ethnicity, who was removed from a managerial post. If that's the question, then yes, indeed, I met the man and I said that he was very much taken aback by that decision. He was the manager of the local post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that, in fact, dismissals of non-Serbs in addition to that man were taking place in Petrovac, whatever you personally felt about it. And you answered: "Yes, they were taking place," and that's correct also?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This happened, for the most part, in companies that were not within the remit of the municipal authorities. I believe that only one or two persons -- I believe it was our head of the accountancy department and somebody else was -- they were, I think, not dismissed but simply put on hold, which meant that their employment contract was still valid and their years of pension would still be accrued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
