utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to be a strange puzzle. Mr. Tieger and I would like to try to understand how the witness could have said that: "We resisted." I think this is what was said. And how did they resist? What happened in point of fact? I'm asking you the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said specifically how this took place, and I used one illustration, and this was a company which had more than 1.000 employees. Prompted by the instructions that were in circulation, and they had to do with the dismissal of the persons who were allegedly disloyal to the establishment of the Republika Srpska, they asked from the municipal authorities to issue them with a decision on the basis of which they would then proceed to dismiss their people. When the president of the Executive Board consulted me on the matter and asked for my opinion, I said that this was unlawful and unacceptable, that we did not have the necessary authority to do that or to issue them with such a decision. And we produced a document to that effect, which I believe is still filed in the municipality of Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who took the decision to terminate the work contract of those employees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who specifically made the decision, but the decision came from this body which was called the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was signed and we received it from them. Now, whether it was made by a body or by an individual, we -- I don't know, but we tried to evade the implementation of the document because we felt that its implementation would be very much detrimental for the municipality, because all these people, if they were later on to lodge a complaint, would win the cases and we would have to pay large indemnities. That's why the municipal body did not want to act upon such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in -- Mr. Radojko, you were asked precisely about that during the course of your Brdjanin testimony. You talked about, on page 20139, how you attempted to get around the order in that -- in the way you described, and then you were asked flatly: "All right. So you didn't approve of the decision, you thought in your view that it was illegal, and you tried to get round it but did you actually implement it?" And you said: "Well, I told you, it was implemented." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent it was implemented. As far as the municipality is concerned, it was implemented in a round-about way. Not in the way which was requested, but rather the persons were put on hold, as it were, which meant that they were not required to come to their work-place, but their work contract was still valid and they would still receive years of pensionable service, which meant that they could not appeal against such a decision; their employment was not terminated. And our approach was to, on the one hand, try and partially implement the decision, but on the other hand to not withhold workers' rights and their salaries and thus pre-empt any action on their part. I believe there were one or two Muslims only who were among the employees, but in this way not only Muslims were dismissed but also Serbs who, for instance, failed to respond to call-ups. So this was not a practice that was aimed solely at the Muslims. The decision was not put in those terms. It also had to do with others. I remember a -- a lady who worked for the land registry office who also was sent back home in this way, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What would have happened if you hadn't implemented the decision? If you had refused? If you had called on, you know, abiding by the law. If you said you have to abide by the law, you have to respect the law, what would have happened? You don't always do what you're ordered to do; sometimes you can resist. So what would have happened if you had said: No, this is illegal, we won't do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in fact there was resistance. Most of the persons working in these companies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but you answered Mr. Tieger. You said: We did apply the order in some manner or another. We applied it. So my question is the following: What would have happened if you had not applied those orders, if you hadn't enforced the orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speculate. I don't know what the balance of powers was; I didn't know that at the time either. It is quite possible that the leadership, that's to say members of Crisis Staff, would have experienced some consequences due to that. I could only answer the question as to whether it was legal or illegal. I wasn't thinking about it at the time as to what sort of subordination they were in, if they were at all. But generally speaking, due to the fact that people were mobilised, nobody was in fact working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you fear consequences if you had resisted, personal consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not my duty either to implement it or not to implement it. I simply did not think about it. Whether the people who had decision-making powers were afraid to implement them, I don't know, because they did not speak their minds in that sense. It is possible that they would have been criticised or punished for failing to implement them. At any rate, they tried to act in such a way that it seems that they implemented, in fact, these documents, although they did not fully agree with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one or two questions in this respect as well. You -- in your answers, you emphasised the aspect that they were not fired, their contracts would still be valid, they even would -- accrued a -- pension rights. That's an interpretation of what happened. Another interpretation could be: We did it in such a way that no legal action could be taken against it because they were not fired, so therefore they were empty-handed as far as legal action is concerned. You gave one interpretation. What made you emphasise this aspect and not -- while considering the other possibility, that it was a very safe way by only partly implementing the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to note -- to point out the following: That municipal offices staff had no reason for instituting legal action. Had they been fired, they would have instituted a legal action and won the case before a court. The solution chosen was the one that would be most favourable also for the staff because, let's say, a lady who was taken -- who was told to go home, she nevertheless had her entitlements. She was still employed but simply did not come to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're repeating your interpretation; you're not answering my question. My question was why - as you do now again emphasise - what could be considered positive for those who were put on hold and why you consider this to be more important than the other side, that is, that they could not take any legal action which would, to some extent, also paralyze them in the situation at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had the possibility, the legal remedy, of appealing such a decision, because at the time, as is still the case today, legal action could also be taken pursuant to such a decision. I believe there was even more possibility of such legal action at the time than is today. When I think back about that, had they lodged a complaint or appealed such a decision, the situation was such that no decision would probably be rendered to their benefit or detriment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say they could have taken action against it, even against this decision. I was trying to find another part of your testimony but I'll do it at a later stage. Could you tell us: Did those who were entitled to pension, did they receive their pensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this must have been an error in interpretation. Nobody had their pension entitlements pursuant to this because we're talking about persons who were my juniors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But later on. I mean, you say it was nice for them because they were put on hold, they would accrue their pension rights. Was none of the persons dismissed or put on hold entitled, to this very moment, to pension rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Serb population was fully chased away from the area in 1995, I lost touch with these persons. Now the pension funds were separated and I don't know what the situation currently is. I suppose that a person from that municipality has had his or her rights to pension recognised. That would only be logical. I believe that the matter is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pension rights are paid at this moment. The portion of your testimony I wanted to confront you with in relation to my last question was where you said: "Their employment was not terminated and our approach was to, on the one hand, try and partially implement the decision, but on the other hand to not withhold workers' rights and their salaries and thus pre-empt any action on their part," which I understood to be that no action could be taken by this halfway implementation. But now you tell us otherwise. You say that they could have taken action. Could you reconcile these two answers and explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour. They were entitled to appeal this decision, but under the circumstances, they felt the decision was favourable. That's why they did not decide to appeal the decision. There was this lady, for instance, who was of Serb nationality. Later on she went to Belgrade and she was replaced by another person who ran the accountancy department. I suppose, for instance, this particular person was first sent home but was then asked to return and resume her post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say and thus pre-empt any action on their part -- well, that's not -- no, I withdraw that question. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, in connection with the Court's question, let's try to clarify that through the use of a particular example. You were asked about all of this during the course of your Brdjanin testimony, and you testified at pages 23 -- 20316 through 20317 about, for example, your recollection of how your boss on one occasion, when asked by a large company about it, instructed you how to put the official answer to their query, "and I did that." Now, although I don't have it in the tabs because I just called it up electronically, it can be broadcast here on -- electronically, I believe, but if not, I will read this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it in evidence already?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P748, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is an inquiry of August 21st from the timber processing company about the status of persons of Muslim nationality. And it says: "In connection with your request to resolve the issue of the status of the persons of Muslim nationality employed in your company, we send you the answer again which consists of the following: Compared to the previous response, there are no changes with regards to the status of persons of Muslim nationality. In that regard, we would like to refer you to the provisions of the decision on stipulating the status of employees number -" and the number is provided - "dated June 22nd, 1992, which was reached at the session of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And as you explained in your testimony in the Brdjanin case, and here I refer to pages 20 -- to page 20345, you knew it was against the law, you didn't want to assume the legal responsibility for it, so you wrote the company and told them: You have to comply with the ARK order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, no. It was something totally different. We said that the Crisis Staff did not have it within its remit to make decisions pertaining to employees. That's the reference to that decision, because what was in that decision - and I know when it was being debated - the conclusion was that the Crisis Staff would not have the remit to do that on their behalf. And that's why the decision was made in this way. I was taking the minutes, and I know that they were grappling with it for a long time and looking for an appropriate solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, the fact is that you told the company to follow the order that you knew was illegal, correct? And you said that in your Brdjanin testimony at the page I noted. Do you want me to read that transcript to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within this context I said that they were asked to do what they deemed fit, because had the Crisis Staff wanted to lend their support to this ARK Krajina decision, they would have done so or said so. They were simply referring to the contents of that decision. And I do remember the discussion within the Crisis Staff because a great deal of time was pinned on trying to find a way to get out of that and for the Crisis Staff not to get involved in any of that. And so those were my instructions. I was trying to draft the appropriate text, and then finally they said: Okay, that's fine. But the main point was that the company in question had to solve their own problems. Apart from that, the relationship between the company in question and the administration were rather bad, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the company had to solve its own problems. The legal responsibility, as far as you saw it, was on its shoulders. And in response to its inquiry to you, to the Crisis Staff, about the status of Muslim employees, you helpfully sent them the ARK order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We instructed them to make their own decisions. The municipality was a separate legal person and issuing such instructions would have been very risky. Even a budget of many years wouldn't have been able to pay for all those complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the ARK decision that was referred to in P748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab number, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe we have this document. I guess I can put it on the ELMO or read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which one would it be so I can find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the Crisis Staff decision of June 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in P748. I've got nine --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour, when I referred to P748, that was the letter that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that makes reference to this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the source of the ARK decision is? If you give me the number, I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate that, Your Honour. Your Honour, I know that this document is in evidence because I recall its use with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm not saying it's not in evidence, I'm just trying to find it in my computer, and therefore I need a number, Mr. Tieger. You can't give it at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm as anxious as I can be for the witness to have it in front of him. It's not satisfactory, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger can read from it. I take it you can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's splendid. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, so you know, this document is going to be -- you can see it next to you, but you'll also be able to see it on your screen, and the usher will assist you in finding the right button. Again, sir, this is the ARK Crisis Staff decision to which you referred the company that inquired about the status of its Muslim employees, and it states the following: "At its meeting of 22 June, 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted the following decision. All executive posts, posts involving a likely flow of information; posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts important for the functioning of economy, may only be held by the personnel of Serbian nationality."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I can now tell the Court that's P358. I'm sorry we weren't able to do so earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radojko, if I can ask you in that connection to turn to tab 55, perhaps we can see the reaction and response of the Petrovac Crisis Staff to that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Already a number, Mr. Tieger, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just a moment. That is P359.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P359, found at tab 55, Mr. Radojko, is a report or letter by Mr. Novakovic of June 25th, 1992, on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Petrovac municipality, sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding the implementation of steps and decisions set in the Crisis Staff session of 22 June 1992. And it makes reference to that decision and informs the ARK Crisis Staff that: "The following steps from item 1 of the decision have been implemented in the territory of our municipality. The steps envisioned in item 1, paragraph 1, of the decision have been implemented in all public enterprises and institutions of public interest and other labour associations as well as public places." And then it goes on: "According to available information, the same steps have been -- have also been implemented in socially owned enterprises. Whereby we lack the most recent information, taking into account that not a single one of our socially owned enterprises or joint stock enterprises has operated for two and a half months due to war circumstances. All members of Muslim nationality, both active and reserved, have been sacked from their jobs at the public security station. Employees of Muslim nationality defined in item 1 of this decision were sacked earlier on from their jobs in the Municipal Assembly administration organs. Remaining employees have been sacked now, with the exception of one employee who was due to complete his tasks but will be sacked after that." Mr. Radojko, that represents the response of the Petrovac Crisis Staff to the ARK order of June 22nd, 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the proviso that certain things here have not been covered. By way of an example, there was an exemption of one employee who was kept on. That one employee, a woman, in fact -- that's fine. Or else it says that these measures are in the process of being implemented, or in the process of being finalised. So that's what I meant to say when I said that they were continually trying to prove that they were implementing those decisions, but those decisions were never fully implemented. For example, the only thing that sticks in my mind is this local post office manager. And at the veterinary station, I think there was somebody else and I think he was replaced by another colleague. And as to other companies, all the leading positions, all the managerial posts were already in the hands of Serbs, at least in as far as the big companies were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were also asked about -- well, you -- during the -- in the course of discussions about -- just prior to the discussion about dismissals in the Brdjanin case you testified that: "Mr. Novakovic personally urged everybody to respect the decisions whether -- that were made, whether they were the military or the Krajina or the Serb Republic." Correct? That's found at page 20137. You won't find that in the tabs, sir, I'm just quoting from your testimony. That's correct, isn't it? Mr. Novakovic, as you testified in the Brdjanin case, personally urged people to respect the decisions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that in relation to certain decisions, that must be the case. I don't know what decisions you're referring to. I can't say because I do not know with reference to what decisions support was given and for which it wasn't. But if I said it back then, then it must have been true because, as far as I can remember, I was shown the decisions and I always replied on the basis of what I saw in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger's summary is unfair yet again. I invite him to read out the whole of the question at 20137, beginning with "Right ..." and the whole answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, especially since the Chamber -- since the transcript is not in evidence, I think we should avoid that Mr. Josse has to ask you to give complete quotes if they are of a difference -- different nature. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am more than happy, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to quote as extensively from the transcript as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just not to get a wrong impression of the testimony of the witness at that time by limiting the quote to a small portion, where nearby more nuance is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Radojko: "Right. Now you say that he wasn't -- Mr. Novakovic wasn't personally subordinated to him in any way or anyone else in Banja Luka. But as we have been going through all these decisions by the Crisis Staff in Petrovac, the decisions made by the regional Crisis Staff, what sort of impact were they having? I mean you refer to them quite a lot." Answer: "I just mentioned what kind of personal relations there were. But I did not -- they did not affect decisively the functioning of the administration and Mr. Novakovic personally urged everybody to respect the decisions regardless of the persons behind them, whether it has to do with the military or the Krajina, that is AR Krajina or the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is if one thought the decisions were purposeful they were put through. Only the decisions which made no sense, which served no purpose, and did not have anything to do with our area, they were not implemented or could not be, especially those which were quite illegal and could therefore entail very grave consequences at a later stage." That's what you testified to, Mr. Radojko, and that was correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked about, as I indicated earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for our understanding, again it's -- we don't have the transcript. Did -- was Mr. Radojko at that time asked to give an example of such a decision that was not implemented because it was quite illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I assist, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am happy that at some later stage -- the answer to Your Honour's question is: Yes, very much so. It is followed up in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am happy for the following passage to come into evidence here. I'll have to work out the logistics with Mr. Tieger later on. If he's happy. If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- it should be put to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would that be agreeable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's fine. And do I understand that the Court doesn't have the transcripts in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't understand that that was the way we were proceeding, and I can deal with that at a later stage. I find this to be an enormously cumbersome and indeed counter-productive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the consequence of you have presented under 92 bis but then later withdrawn this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I never suggested that that should be in evidence, but the idea that a document to which I'm referring cannot be in front of the Court at the point at which I'm referring to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it could not be, but when a document is not in evidence anymore, the Chamber will not keep it under its arms for the rest of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course not. I'm merely asking if the Court has it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have no Brdjanin transcripts in front of us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did not understand that to be the case, and I respectfully suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would help, then we would read subsequent portions of it. May I take it -- let's proceed. And if during the next break you and Mr. Josse -- we could have that break now, for example -- could agree upon how to proceed and we at least could read matters together with you, then fine. Perhaps I leave it to the parties at this moment and have a break anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. We've no objection to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Us reading --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- Your Honour having the passages that are quoted. I do have some concerns about reading on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would have to look carefully whether we turn the page, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I do understand. But of course I do understand your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I merely want to point out that that is a reversal of an approach that was adopted and used in this courtroom before with, I think, the full support of the Defence and full knowledge of the Defence. Now, suddenly, these documents are being withdrawn from the Court as if we're engaged in a -- in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Withdrawn, withdrawn --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not withdrawn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We put them aside since they were not in evidence anymore, but we have read them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't mean that to sound more dramatic than it was. What I simply meant was in the past the Court has had such interviews, statements, available to it for the purpose of assisting it in asking any questions that might be relevant. Everyone knows that, and I -- I didn't understand that we had embarked on a retreat from that approach. And I don't think there's any basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I invite you to see whether any solution could be found during the next break, where we will resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any resolution of the problem on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I invite the -- based on our discussions, I invite the registrar to distribute the transcripts to the Bench. Mr. Josse may have some comments in connection with that, but I'm pleased that we were able to resolve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this is the Defence position: Of course we've got no objection to the Chamber following the cross-examination, the passages that are put. To object to that would, we concede, be nonsensical. We would invite the Court not to look beyond the passages that are put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. On the basis of the procedural history, you would say this was a -- and I understand a 92 bis witness, has been withdrawn, now not the whole of the evidence should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And thereafter, when the witness is finished his evidence, effectively, with respect, we would invite the Court to hand back the volumes. Because the matter -- those passages that have been put to the witness will then be in evidence, depending on his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, so far as the issue that Your Honour has raised, which is whether or not there are any follow-up questions in relation to the last matter my learned friend was examining upon, I have agreed to deal with those in my re-examination. They are quite lengthy passages, let me say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber accepts the proposed procedure. I add to that that one could wonder where the evidence was not admitted because it seems that the Prosecution was not in a position to call the witness for cross-examination, that we find ourselves in a bit of an odd position. But the Chamber has accepted the -- the suggested procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I needn't mention, because I'm sure this is at the forefront of Your Honour's mind, we've called the witness, we've not been able to cross-examine him, that's why the Defence on this occasion are being so particular about the procedure adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One could ask oneself the strict rules on the difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination, to what extent they should be maintained in this court, but let's not start that discussion now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, if I could ask you to turn to tab 56, please, and it's P90, tab 27. The minutes of the Petrovac Crisis Staff from June 13th, 1992, and if I could ask you, sir, to turn to the decision which is reflected on page 4 of the English, and it's the fifth decision, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 3 in the B/C/S, I take it, under the first "Odluku," Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Starting with VP 4452.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, that's the decision that begins with a reference to the postal service being completely disconnected from Bihac and continues: "The Petrovac post office body in charge will cut a number of telephone users and disconnect 800 numbers from the Petrovac telephone service. When disconnecting, it has to ensure that the proper functioning of economical, administrative and military bodies and organisations is not jeopardised." Mr. Radojko, that's a decision which is also reflected in your diary for the date of 13 June. I believe it's found at pages 83 through 84. And your diary reflects the following: "Disconnection of telephones of all Muslims, removing them from all key positions, particularly in the communications system." And your diary also contains a reference to the same decision about the post office as well. So the Crisis Staff order to disconnect 800 telephone users was a decision to disconnect the telephones of Muslim telephone users. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Most of the users, telephone service users mentioned here are in fact Muslims. There was general mistrust about phones being tapped. For instance, there was one physician and -- or rather, President Karadzic himself had suspicion that, in fact, his consulting rooms had been tapped. There were efforts at solving the conflict peacefully that went on for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in that respect. Is cutting off Muslims from the telephone connections, is that a measure which would assist in preventing tapping of non-Muslim telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the technical details involved. At any rate, outside of what is being -- was written in the minutes and in my notes, I can tell you that they acted this way for safety reasons because they were afraid that the Muslims were relaying some important information. In this way, they wanted to hinder, in a way, the conveyance of such information, if not to prevent any such conveyance altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, can we turn next to tab 29, which reflect the minutes of the 34th session of the Petrovac Crisis Staff of June 14th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radojko, this is another document that you were -- that you testified about during the course of your appearance in the Brdjanin case. That can be found at pages 20134 and 20135. And you were asked the following: "All right. Just to look at -- I don't think this time you did attend the meeting. Yes, I'm sorry, the meeting in Korcanica. Okay. Now, then, we see that Mr. Vrzina reported on the situation in the municipality and conveyed the brigade command's request that Muslims be excluded from the work of the Municipal Assembly administrative organs and that arrested persons suspected on reasonable grounds of participating in undermining the Serbian Republic defence or preparing an attack on its institutions and citizens should not be released from detention before trial." And that's reflected in item 1 of the minutes. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question goes on: "And then requested that Muslim inhabitants who had pledged loyalty to the Serbian Republic be included in defence preparations. "So again, the military was reinforcing what it had said the previous day, about Muslims effectively being excluded and, indeed -- well, excluded. Is that right?" And your answer was: "Yes. It is right. The army never stopped putting pressure. They had learned that there was an intention to form a unit made of Muslims and incorporate it in the defence, and they opposed it. And also when he talks about these detainees, Mr. Gacesa, who was the chief of police, said -- and I don't think you can find it in the minutes -- told the president that the police practically had no evidence against the majority of those detainees and that they would have to release them, and of course, the members of the military command learned about that and they spread this information around the units on the front and therefore the pressure not to release them, so this conclusion is not based on law, but it is a factual conclusion." All that information is correct, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, could you please answer whether it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct. The pressure was exerted, and that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radojko, do you understand English or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a little bit, but when one speaks fast, I cannot really follow at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll not speak fast. Could you please take your earphones off for a second. Some -- when we're talking about pressure, some pressure is put upon me to decide on whether we are sitting tomorrow, yes or no. Mr. Tieger, could you tell me approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to gauge. We -- I'm -- I would ask the Court to keep that possibility open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time other Presiding Judges are fighting for -- I just want to know how much time you think you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll certainly need the remainder of this session and I -- based on the pace, I think I'm going to need another session after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it -- I take it from what you said earlier that you would need some time for re-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, some time, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would one session tomorrow be sufficient, because then I could give a message to other Trial Chambers that some time would remain tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Clearly, Your Honour, I would be in a better position to gauge that at the end of this session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can't delay. I don't know how much time Mr. Josse would need, but if the Court could give a little longer than one session, that would be safest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then most likely there what would not be two sessions left tomorrow for any other Trial Chamber. Less than that. Let's see how far we can come. Mr. Radojko, please put your earphones on again. To the extent you were able to follow, you may conclude that we'll not finish your testimony today, unfortunately, perhaps for you. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, can I ask you to turn next to tab 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which also needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 30, Your Honours, would be P1103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if you could just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, tab 30, P1103, contains the minutes of the 35 session of the -- 35th session of the Petrovac municipality Crisis Staff, held on June 16th, 1992, and it reflects in item 1 the president indicating that: "The Crisis Staff was expected to formulate a clear position on the Muslims and that the military demanded that such measures be taken against them as would make it impossible for them to undertake actions and organise in our forces' rear." It continues --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of counsel and the Court, he testified about this on pages 20142 and 20143 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Gacesa stressing: "... that there was a list of some 40 people or so considered to be organised as a separate group or to have acted from extreme fundamentalist Islamic positions. Of these, 13 are already out of the reach of law enforcement organs. The operation to disarm Muslims paramilitary units and citizens is continuing. Most of the persons included in the above-mentioned list have been found to possess illegal weapons. There are two possible options, one, that a certain number of persons, who could be a potential threat, be isolated but not on the premises of the SJB, and the other, that extremists be located -- be isolated outside of Petrovac." "Mr. Vrzina considered that the second option was more acceptable. "As the discussion continued, the view prevailed that the isolation of extremists outside Petrovac would be dangerous to themselves, and that it was best to isolate them in a well-guarded facility on the outskirts of town." And then it concludes with a decision: "All individuals who possess illegal weapons or have been registered as Muslim extremists, thus posing a potential threat, shall be detained and held in custody." Now, at page 20143, Mr. Radojko, you were asked: "Now, what was this register of Muslim extremists?" And you answered: "Officially, such a register could not be established. To the best of my knowledge this was done on the basis of initial operative knowledge obtained by the police themselves. Some people did indeed have weapons that were found, as far as I know, and other people were put on this list according to their own arbitrary assessments. You see, when they say here that -- that the 13 are inaccessible, these are people who had already left the territory of the municipality." So these minutes of June 16th, Mr. Radojko, according to your testimony in the Brdjanin case, reflect the detention of Muslims who were either found to have illegal weapons or were detained according to what you referred to as arbitrary assessments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's correct. Nobody was able to keep accurate records of those who allegedly were extremists. Only those who were found to have illegal weapons could have been established as such. Other than that, the only way to approach the matter was through assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were asked thereafter about a couple of people who you knew had been detained, including Fuad Ferizovic, and you indicated that you and Mr. Ferizovic did not agree about certain legal positions and things like that, but you thought that he was considered to be an extremist because he presented some kind of radical claims perhaps in a political sense. This did not correspond to what people really liked to hear, but you personally had discussions with him without any problems whatsoever. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did I also understand you to be criticising these arbitrary assessments when you made the comment in connection with Mr. Ferizovic on page 20145: "If somebody just says something a bit sharply, I don't think that he should be called an extremist."

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was presenting my viewpoint, which is, I believe, logical. You cannot call someone an extremist on the sole basis of what he says. At the time, this notion of extremism wasn't as well-known to everyone as it is today. I don't know what the criteria were for defining what these people were. I knew that there was reason to distrust persons who were found to have illegal weapons. There was another case that was conducted at the time which involved a lady member of staff who worked with me. Her father was kept in custody for a short while, and she intervened with the president of the Executive Board who inquired into the matter and asked that the man be released. You have to know that I wasn't -- I did not originate from this place and I didn't know the people. I wasn't familiar with their viewpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn next to tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P748, tab 5, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, in order not to forget that, you asked for a number of the 35th meeting of the -- oh, no, no, no. Yes, let me just have a look. No, please proceed, I'm greatly mistaken, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 31, Mr. Radojko, contains the minutes of the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- no, I -- I'm too critical for myself, Mr. Tieger. The 35th meeting of the Crisis Staff of Petrovac municipality, 16th of June, K5792, you asked for a number, but P90HH, and perhaps even P90BB as well - but let me just check on the latter one - seem to be the same documents, and from what I understand there are even different versions of that document. So would you please find that out. Not at this very moment but soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will double-check that, but preliminary checking seems to indicate the Court is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I can tell you that the version we find under 90BB seems to cover the same -- I only have the English translation -- well, there seem to be different versions of that document as well, so would you please keep that in mind as well; with numbers, without numbers, with different signatures, et cetera. So would you please pay attention to that and at this moment proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and we will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I had directed your attention to the Petrovac Crisis Staff minutes for the session held on June 17th, 1992. As previous documents we looked at indicated, there was a discussion about whether to retain the prisoners, the Muslim prisoners, in the SJB or send them outside Petrovac. If I could ask you to turn to the third decision of the Crisis Staff, found at page 4 of the English, which indicates the following -- and I think you'll have no trouble finding that. I believe that's the second page of your version. "On the level on the 2nd Krajina Corps, the prisoners from the Petrovac public security station are to be transferred to Prekaja or to Manjaca. "The Crisis Staff discussed at this session the question of security situation and the supplies in the territory of the municipality and the question of status --" and it goes on to -- "... the question of status of the Territorial Defence conscripts, and accordingly adopted the following ..." and then we see a subject related -- or a decision related to a subject we covered before, Muslim owners of bars, restaurants, and shops are to temporarily close. But turning back to the decision I referred to earlier, it's correct then that the decision was made on June 17th, 1992, that the prisoners from the Petrovac public security station were to be transferred to one of those two detention facilities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content is right, but this was not, in fact, done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's follow through and look at some of the other subsequent decisions that were made, or decisions being made around that time to see what happened to those prisoners. If you'll turn to tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe this needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 33, Your Honours, would be P1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1104, found at tab 33, Mr. Radojko, is a strictly confidential 2nd Krajina Corps command order on forming prisoner of war camps. And it states that: "Pursuant to the document of the Main Staff of the Army of Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, strictly confidential -" provides the number - "from 12 June 1992 and based on indicated needs, I order -" and then it indicates a number of facilities - that: "A prisoner of war camp is to be formed in the area of the railway settlement Srnetica. In the first phase, until the required facilities in Srnetica are fully arranged, prisoners of war are to be accommodated in the facilities of the forestry workers' settlement Kozila and the school in Kamenica." Now, first of all, before I ask you about that, it may be helpful to note that this Court has -- this document makes reference to an order of 12 June 1992 and this Court has received in evidence a 12 June 1992 order, number 18/28-6, by General Mladic regarding the establishments -- establishment of camps, prisoners of war detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's found at P64A, Your Honour. Sorry, I thought I had the tab number, and if not, I will provide that for the Court as soon as possible. Sorry, Your Honour, we'll have to get the tab number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's P64A, binder is 27, footnote 783 is where the Mladic order can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, were you aware of the arrangement to have prisoners taken to the -- to a facility in Kozila until other facilities might be established?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I have under binder 7, I have another numbering not related to footnote, but sequence within tab 7 goes from 1 to 27. If you could help me out which one. I think that's also the way it was -- I see your case manager can't help me at this moment. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, were you familiar with the use of Kozila as a detention facility for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that such an order existed. I know that there was a detention centre in Kozila, which was provisional, and I don't think it had to do anything with this order. This was, I believe, pursuant to a police order that they decided to organise detention there. But these were private homes and this was in Petrovac because Petrovac did not have a detention unit of its own, it had only these private homes, and they gave up the idea of detaining people there and decided to put the people up at Kozila because this was a workers' housing development. I believe that they wanted to put there those people who were found to possess illegal weapons or were otherwise characterised as extremists. They were not prisoners of war of any sort. They were kept there for a while and were then released. After that, they had to, I believe, report to the police that they were still around. I know this because of another issue: When representatives of the International Red Cross came over from Knin, they asked to be allowed to see those people. The president of the Executive Board told me to talk to them. As they arrived quite late in the day, we were unable to go over to see the facility. They were afraid of travelling by night, so they had to leave for Knin quite early and they were to return the day -- the next day. However, the next day there was an order issued for the people to be released. So there was nobody to visit there anymore. But I know for a fact that these persons were not prisoners of war, they were people from the town. To the best of my knowledge, but I'm not sure, I believe it was the police that took them into custody and not the army, certainly not pursuant to this order. Although I don't know in what way the police and the army operated, what their relations were, I only know what sort of people were there because I was supposed to lead a delegation to see the facility on the morning during which in fact the people were released. I also know this because this -- the father of this colleague of mine, Ferizovic, complained about the fact that he had been beaten by some of the guards there, and he was not a prisoner of war; I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's turn next, if we can, to tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's, I hope, P90, tab 33; P529, tab 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are the minutes of the 41st Session of the Petrovac Crisis Staff, Mr. Radojko, held on 29 June, 1992. Begins in item 1 with Mr. Novakovic, who in the second paragraph relayed requests from soldiers he had talked to for a more radical attitude towards the Muslims at Petrovac. Continues that: "The Muslims of Petrovac are behaving as if they are wounded and are showing great fear. More of them should be arrested and isolated as a precaution, after which they should be given work obligations because there will be a lot of harvesting to do." And then if we turn to the conclusions, conclusion number 1 is the following: "Until the prison in Kozila is made operational, a plan should be made to arrest and bring in under custody all Muslims fit for military service who are thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Serbs. "And the persons responsible: Obrad Vrzina and Drago Gacesa." Now, Obrad Vrzina is the military representative and Drago Gacesa is the police representative; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And together they were responsible for taking these -- for ensuring that all Muslims fit for military service who were thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Muslims were taken into custody. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make a correction? My understanding is to the detriment of Serbs on the basis of these minutes. And here we are talking about these people who were found in possession of weapons and who were considered and proclaimed to be fundamentalists, not all able-bodied Muslims but only those amongst their fundamentalists, and so that's what it's all about and that part was implemented. I was present, but since Mr. Sikman -- or basically, I was invited to attend the meeting but I didn't -- I wasn't in charge of the minutes. I mean, I was normally in charge of the minutes because I was always at hand; I lived in the vicinity. But on this occasion, he was there so I had nothing to do with the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a correct -- previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again interrupt for the practical matter I raised earlier. Mr. Josse, I'm also looking at you. If we would have a late start tomorrow in the afternoon, if we would have a late start --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would have a late start tomorrow in the afternoon, that means starting at a quarter to 5.00, and then have two one-hour sessions with a 15-minute break, from what you said before, it looks as if that would -- a little bit over one session would be sufficient, or would it not, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be -- I hope I'm not -- it's difficult to tell. We make considerable progress sometimes and then there's always the chance of a significant issue that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Takes more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, is worth the time we invest in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make this observation: I was thinking about this at the very moment Your Honour raised the subject. I -- perhaps the witness should take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radojko, would you please take your earphones off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I curtailed my examination-in-chief. I also had my preparation with the witness curtailed necessarily. I'm not complaining about that. The result is that Mr. Tieger is spending a great deal of time with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am inclined to have -- to re-examine for a lengthy period of time. That's a present thought going through my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will, with some apologies, deny any request from other Trial Chambers and just claim the time tomorrow, as is available to us, and not try to fit matters in. What you just said, Mr. Josse, of course raises another issue about the 60 per cent guideline. And I'd like to make one observation. Much of this material is in evidence. Of course you never know how a witness would respond to those documents, but if they would remain in evidence without giving any opportunity, it might not be favourable for the accused to have them in evidence and not to have given any opportunity for further explanations, et cetera. That is why the Chamber is granting a bit more time -- of course it is your choice on whether or not to deal with these documents, especially those who are in evidence already; sometimes they are related one to another, but therefore the Chamber is a bit hesitant to either curtail the Prosecution, but also to curtail the Defence in re-examination and therefore does not accept the two hours of tomorrow, but at least make sure that all the time that was reserved for this Trial Chamber is available for it tomorrow. I see Mr. Registrar is phoning already, to the disappointment, perhaps, of some other Trial Chambers. Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no observation in relation to that at this stage. Matter of proceeding in this particular manner, we will contemplate it, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radojko, this document was presented to you during the Brdjanin case as well, and you testified about that in particular at page 20158 and 20159. And you were asked under -- referring to the document: "Under conclusions until the prison in Kozila is made operational a plan should be made to arrest and bring in under custody all Muslims fit for military service who are thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Serbs and then the persons responsible. So this conclusion was anybody fit for -- any military-age Muslim should be brought in. Is that what happened? "Why, no, but able-bodied, those who could perhaps end up doing something wrong, that is some people perhaps for those -- who places weapons on -- whose places weapons were found and another group perhaps just arbitrarily pin-pointed by the police or those army people. I do not know how they did that, but I think it was done on the basis of whatever condition -- convictions that they may have been upholding at the time rather than on the basis of some reliable facts." And that accurately reflected your understanding at the time of these events. Is that correct, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we turn to tab 22, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 22, Your Honour, is P90, tab 36. And that is a list of persons for whom Bosanski Petrovac public security station has ordered isolation and indicates at the bottom that a total of 29 persons who were taken to do labour at the Kozila camp on July 1st, 1992. And on the following page is a list of July 2nd, 1992, with a list of persons to be handed over to the Kozila civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Mr. Radojko, that both lists contain the names of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that both lists contain the names of Muslims, but I believe that CZ doesn't mean civil protection but central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate -- thank you for that correction, sir. Can we turn back now to tab 29. We've looked at that previously. That's the minutes of the Crisis Staff -- of Petrovac Crisis Staff from 14th June 1992. And Mr. Novakovic opened the session, and this was a portion of the document that was not referred to earlier. "Mr. Novakovic opened the discussion and pointed out that it was necessary to adopt positions at the level of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on how to deal with inhabitants who were not loyal to the Serbian Republic of BH." And the conclusion, on the next page, was that: "The president of the Petrovac Crisis Staff will request at a session of the Crisis Staff of Krajina Autonomous Region that positions be adopted regarding re-settlement of the population, the inclusion of loyal Muslims in the system of defence, the work of Muslims in administrative organs and companies, and the treatment of persons who have not pledged their loyalty or who have taken hostile positions." So by mid-June 1992, Mr. Radojko, the Petrovac Crisis Staff was considering and seeking guidance about the re-settlement of the population. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. Obviously they asked for guidance in relation to all that, and I believe that they acted in line with this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we had earlier looked at the minutes of the 30 June Crisis Staff in which it was related that the army wanted a more radical attitude toward Muslims. If I could ask you to turn to tab 38, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if you can give me a moment. My version of tab 38 is incomplete. I think I have another version available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 38 seems to be P90, tab 37. Could we try to have that P90, tab 37 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do have a version that we could put on the ELMO, Your Honour, including the -- and I have a B/C/S version I could present to the witness. I don't know if his version is complete or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the minute of the 42nd Session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A copy could be printed out from the electronic version, if need be. Could it be put on the ELMO so that I can just verify that we have the right document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The B/C/S version, Your Honour, is in the bundle; it's the English that's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the English one, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please -- there's one page missing, I take it, or two pages missing. Could you please print out the first two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness could be given the B/C/S version if he -- oh, it's in the bundle as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, turning to item 1 of the session of the Crisis Staff held on July 1st, again we see Obrad Vrzina is the military representative, and he's reporting on the security situation on the territory of the municipality and assessed it as "delicate with a popular feeling of discontent, especially directed toward Muslims after the recent events on the front line and stressed that the best and the sure solution for the protection of the Muslims would be to move the population." So this, by -- or on July 1st, this is the military now urging the moving out of the Muslim population as a means of dealing with the situation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army asked that not on the 1st of July, at least a representative relayed it in that way. They were exerting a great deal of pressure constantly, as you can see on the basis of all these documents. There is a new element that you might have missed here. You can see that there is a certain number of people listed here as having been detained at Kozila and are from Kljuc. And now this has just occurred to me for the first time because the first time around maybe I missed that. Here we're talking about real POWs because at that time back then, as I remember, there were -- there was fighting in Kljuc and Sanski Most municipalities, and the Serb units managed to scatter the enemy units. And many people were going through the Grmec area in the direction of Bihac in order to set up their brigades again. Maybe that made the attitude a little bit more radical, but you can see on a permanent basis, and we can't argue with that and I don't need to repeat this once again, that the command representative constantly came up with very strict requests and in no uncertain terms, and the language used was much more powerful than what you can see in the minutes, because I never used rude words in the minutes for the sake of appearances. But I believe that the president was even trying to use his own channels in order to gauge the actual mood amongst the soldiers and the morale because these requests are very persistent and very sharp and strict. They simply had no understanding for any reasonable explanation, according to which this was just not the way to do things. The president at a certain point even turned to me and asked to come up with a legal solution on the basis of which people could be isolated in some kind of village or whatever. This place that is referred to here is an abandoned housing district, and they were looking for a legal solution in order for people to be legally moved to this place called Srnetica but I had a talk with people about the Americans dealing with the Japanese, et cetera, but of course I said to them that they had to have guards, et cetera, and then it came up that he could not provide reliable guards guarding these people so that they don't come to any harm, and so they desisted from that idea. Not everybody was disloyal amongst the Muslim population. Most people probably didn't care, you know, and many people said openly that they didn't care who was in power, that they were just normal citizens, and they acted that way. So people were different and they opted for different types of behaviour and different allegiances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just look quickly at tab 37. Tab 37, Mr. Radojko, which is P90, tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I didn't realise my phone was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why, Mr. Radojko --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply forgot, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know Presiding Judges who would immediately seize them, but I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been warned, Your Honour, but I simply forgot. It slipped my mind. It's off now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it so it will not be in the collection of seized mobile phones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radojko, this is a document that you had an opportunity -- well, first of all, I should indicate what the document is. It is a report on the events in Bosanski Petrovac from June 1992 until the departure from Petrovac, prepared by the Bosanski Petrovac Expatriots Club. And it's a document that you have had a chance to see before. In fact, you were asked about it during the course of your Brdjanin testimony, and specifically asked at page 20193, whether you had an opportunity to read through it when it was shown to you, and you answered: "I had the opportunity and I read it carefully." And then you were asked: "In your view, is this an accurate account of events as it affected the Muslims in Bosanski Petrovac?" And you answered: "This is a -- an accurate account of events. It is possible that certain details are not quite accurate, but not deliberately, but simply because they didn't know the facts. But yes, it is correct." And that's accurate, sir, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I don't know about all of these events, but the ones I know about are recorded appropriately. I heard of some events from other sources and I suppose that in line with that interpretation they can be considered in the same light, and as to the most recent ones that I'm not familiar with and I saw them for the first time on that occasion, I suppose they're recorded in the proper way. There might be some nuances, but generally speaking this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering that I do accept their impression that they were victimised by the authorities, this is incorrect. But of course they will have that impression in case the authorities did not provide proper protection. Of course they would mistrust the intentions of such authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that last answer be clarified, because I don't think it makes any sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify -- I'll not put to you how I understood it, but, Mr. Radojko, could you please clarify your last answer which says that you do "accept their impression that they were victimised by the authorities. This is incorrect, but of course they will have that impression in case the authorities did not provide proper protection. Of course they will mistrust the intention of such authorities." That's not entirely clear to, at least, Mr. Josse. Could you please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, what I consider as appropriately recorded are facts with regard to individual murders, detention, the departure of those delegations in order to seek authorisation to pass through. All that, in my view, is correct. The only thing is that this bit that in September there was an increasing tension and different methods employed by the Serb authorities in order to encourage Muslims to emigrate, well, that was not my impression, because I was taking the minutes at the Crisis Staff meetings and the documents indicate that the trend was not moving in that direction. It was not our wish to encourage collective emigration, and it caused all sorts of economic difficulties and difficulties in terms of keeping their property safe and millions of other negative consequences. They -- in case such huge numbers of people were to leave. We knew that, even back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that you'll take the witness to further such documents? He says: Looking at the -- taking the minutes of the Crisis Staff meetings, et cetera. We -- of course we have seen already quite some, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- certainly, if I understood that to be -- I will be more -- no, I hadn't intended to. I understood that to be a reference to the -- well, it doesn't matter what I understood it to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that statement to be in this instance, but I had not intended to take him to Crisis Staff minutes that corresponded to that moment in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, sufficient clarification, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll finish for the day. Perhaps some -- I think, as a matter of fact, that I found the first page of tab 38 as the last page of tab 37, Mr. Josse, which might assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I've discovered that. I've also been assisted by the registrar in that regard and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Monday, is the Chamber in a position to inform the parties about Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, about -- perhaps if we first ask the witness to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher. May I instruct you, Mr. Radojko -- may I instruct you, the same as I did yesterday, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. We'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon and then we will finish your examination as a witness. Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next Monday, we are talking about Witness Maricic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have considered your request, Mr. Josse, and the Chamber does not oppose to hear the evidence of Mr. Maricic, as you suggested. At the same time, looking at the 65 ter summary, it causes some concern with the Chamber. If, for example, the 65 ter summary reads: "The conduct of Brcko Serbs was not the result of any instructions from above ..." then of course the Chamber would expect in the 65 ter summary also to find what was his position at the relevant time. Now, the 65 ter summary tells us what his position was in 1994, not in 1992. Therefore, whether this witness would be in a position to tell us that the conduct of Brcko Serbs, whatever that is, I take it that you had in mind the conduct of Brcko Serbs in a more or less organised or disorganised way, but at least not every individual Serb in Brcko, then of course we are wondering what would be the basis for this witness to be able to testify -- at least in the 65 ter summary we find no specific reasons why this witness would be the one who could tell all of this. Similarly, if the 65 ter summary says Mr. Krajisnik never had any command functions over the army and the witness never saw any order issued by Mr. Krajisnik in relation to it, et cetera, et cetera, of course one would not expect an average citizen to have such information about 1992. So not knowing what his position was at that time, was he an ordinary citizen of Brcko, was he not? I mean, if we would call all ordinary citizens of Brcko to tell us whether they'd ever seen any order written by Mr. Krajisnik, then it might take a lot of time. It might not bring that much. So if this -- although I do understand that this witness was listed on the between 10 and 20. If on the basis of this 65 ter summary the Chamber has great difficulties in fully comprehending that this is in the -- but just based on the 65 ter summary, that this is the most important evidence, as the Chamber said before, the Chamber would like to hear as much of as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's our concern. But nevertheless, the Chamber, of course, is limited to the 65 ter summary and if there would have been more information on which you made this selection for this witness, then of course the Chamber would expect that to appear in any updated 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So Your Honour is asking us not to call him or ordering us not to call him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, this is not an order. First of all, the Chamber is aware that we are limited to the 65 ter summary. The Chamber expresses some concern about the importance of the witness, as we can see it from the 65 ter summary. Since the Chamber wants to hear as much evidence as important as possible for the Defence case in the limited time that remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know it's late now. I think Mr. Stewart has the information that Your Honour requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have one piece of information which I feel is likely to be helpful. Just as Your Honour has been speaking I have been bringing up material that I have about Mr. Maricic. Your Honour, I can't say now why it wasn't in the 65 ter, but he joined the SDS in July 1990 and became a member of its Main Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That already makes quite some difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I thought I would tell Your Honours that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course you are asking us -- you are seeking our guidance and we have to give the guidance on the basis of what we see. Therefore you expressed concerns not to say that everyone who was on the Main Board would qualify to be on the top ranking of most important and most relevant evidence, but we'll hear then -- it's clear, at least, that you understood what the Chamber wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We very much understood Your Honour's point. We just thought that might be a helpful piece of single information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, finally, it's your responsibility, of course, first of all, to bring the most important evidence, but at the same time the Chamber is eager to hear what could objectively be understood as vital -- vital evidence and vital information for the Defence case. Then we will adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always speak slowly so that you can say something, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The issue we were concerned about was whether the Court's going to sit on Monday morning. That was what I was alluding to when I rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an answer right away, but I'll -- the first thing I'll do when I've left this courtroom to find out what progress has been made on the inquiry into whether we could sit next Monday in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll be in the building for at least half an hour, so if one of Your Honour's staff could communicate with us, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hope they're still there, the ones who know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
